That means getting beyond certain progressive hangups about race and American history. That does not mean denying the existence of ugly episodes in the country’s story, but it does mean denying the claim that this ugliness defines America or that it is somehow unique to our country rather than part of a perennial pattern of ethnic conflict in human history.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">My ancestors immigrated well before Jerusalem’s and did so at a time when the borders were generally more open but there was also more comfort with heavy-handed assimilation measures. These are deep, profound questions that Americans should and will disagree about forever, and Ogles is dead wrong to insist that any religion is out of bounds. But part of a liberal society is promoting a culture of liberalism. If numerically small sects such as the Amish or Hasidic Jews want to form insular, illiberal faith communities, there’s no issue there. That felt at the time that that was a very older-person access to, you know what I mean?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>iPhone in 2008 was quite expensive.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Yeah. And also just, like, you wouldn’t give your kid something like that. It just is not — it felt kind of weird to me. And also, like, there was, like, of course, the birth rate was falling even before then.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And there’s, like, a very random weird thing where there’s, like, a null effect for Black women for some reason. And I just have — there’s not really an explanation for why that would be. Like, why would the iPhone not affect Black women’s fertility? Like, just seems kind of weird.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, like, I — again, like, this — I’m not an economist. I did not, like, go through this with, like, a rigorous, like, eye to detail.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I would buy that, like, largely every single thing which makes it easier for people not to talk to each other and instead have fun at home alone would, like, reduce fertility rate because it will reduce partnering. And so, like, that has that effect.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Like, if you’re just, like, not going to a party and you’re staying at home and watching TV, that necessarily means you’re not having sex either. And so you’re not gonna have a kid.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And so, like, that all, like, makes sense to me as, like, a broader story here. But, like, I just think it’s really interesting to think about the U.S. in the context of the rest of the world.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Like, the iPhone has spread, or smartphones have spread, basically universally at this point. And yet you still see, like, large variations in birth rates, even if you do see kind of, like, a large-scale decline in most countries. But the fact that there is difference indicates to me that, like, technology is interacting with culture in some way that is, I think, right now, still kind of unexplained.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>So I tried to develop a sophisticated methodological critique of this paper.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>No dice?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>No, no. I think it may just be wrong.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Oh, really? Why?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>I mean, the problem is that…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Oh yeah, there’s also a porn — one of the, part of the…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Well, so they’ve tried to bolster it with this porn thing. But the question of where AT&T coverage existed during this time period is not a random subsample of the United States, right?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span> T&T is a big company. They can count. And so they made sure that their network is really good in the Boston-Washington corridor, all across the Pacific Coast, all throughout Florida, in the Texas Triangle, in the Chicago-Milwaukee Great Lakes population center.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And then it’s very spotty in rural America. You know, they kind of got to it late. They — depending on how close you were to cities. There’s a part of rural Texas that’s just between the big cities, and it has coverage. Also, AT&T as a company is headquartered in Texas, so their coverage there is better than elsewhere.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The authors of this paper are aware of this, that it could just be an urban-rural split. And they’re doing a lot of math to try to counteract this. I think there’s always a question when you deal with that kind of thing of, “Is it working?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Because there’s a million different papers which claim to show that there’s a large causal impact of — sometimes it’s NAFTA, sometimes it’s opioids — on voting for Republicans. But these are all just different ways of reiterating that Ohio swung a lot to the right during a specific 10-year period. Because, like, a lot of different things happened in Ohio during that span of time. And it’s — it’s just challenging.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>It’s difficult. It’s difficult to do this.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>It’s a hard problem because you can’t say what is co-correlating with what.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They show that, you know, as people get smartphones, they access internet porn more. So that’s, like, a plausible hypothesis. But then, as you say, why would early — early iPhone adoption was not concentrated among teenagers, right? Like, that’s not true. So, what are we really getting at here?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think — and the effect size that they find is so big, right? And it doesn’t — that, you know, these things pick up because, like, it sounds true that smartphones have led to, like, less coupling and maybe less sex and maybe fewer babies, but, like, 50% of the…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>It’d be kind of incredible if it was true.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Right. Like, that’s just — that’s a lot. And I don’t know, man. You know, it’s kind of, like, you know, it makes the paper more interesting if you have these kind of high-end impacts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I did want to say, in the teen question, though, it’s not so much — I mean, the impact is negative across the age spectrum, which is different from — you know, you might think, I mean, when I was a teen, there was a lot of, like, anti-teen pregnancy messaging. And I took it at the time, at least, that, like, the goal of that messaging was to, like, shift people’s fertility plans forward. If that messaging caused a large decline in the teen birth rate and a small decline in the 20-something birth rate and still a decline in 30-somethings, you would say, “OK, something has gone wrong with them.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Like, well, there’s more births in the 30 range now.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>There are, but — but they’re saying that their estimate of the causal impact of the iPhone is negative across the entire spectrum, but concentrated in teens, which is different from saying, you know, it just, like, shifted people, right? Because we do see that shift happening, which is, you know, fertility treatments and different life plans, so on and so forth.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So they’re not — They are saying that the iPhone is just moving you uniformly negative, even if it’s concentrated among teenagers. But I don’t know.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>I always have a hard time with these papers, because I’m just, like, “Yeah, it probably seems good if people spend less time on their smartphones.” Like, just, like, I’m just gonna go ahead and say, like, that seems correct.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>You’ve become a weird phone abstentionist.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Yeah, I have my — but I do think that, like, it’s fine to be, like, “I think iPhones or smartphones in general are, like, bad for you” without having to, like, buy these, like, really big stories about how they’re causing, like, every problem in the universe. So I’m just, like, you know, I just, like…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think this often gets cast between, like, you’re, like, a pro-smartphone, like, Taylor Lorenz, believes it’s caused all the benefits of all humanity to accrue to people who get these devices, versus, like, the Jonathan Haidts where, like, it’s causing every single problem known to man.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And I’m, like, you know, I’m gonna say this: Seems bad in general but has some positives in some cases. And, like, if everyone used it less, that seems like it would be largely good.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>I just wonder with some of this stuff, you know, I think there’s a theory that the printing press, like, caused Protestantism, which in turn caused the Thirty Years’ War. And so, all these people died. So that’s bad.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On the other hand, a lot of important long-term benefits accrued from the printing press. On the third hand, if your takeaway from, like, the downsides of the printing press was, like, “We shouldn’t have books in our house,” that actually wouldn’t shelter you from the Thirty Years’ War at all.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>No, for sure. But I just mean, like, I think that there are individual harms to being on the smartphone a lot. Like, I don’t know, like, I just watch parents on their phones next to their children. I’m, like, that seems bad all the time. Like, you know?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Yeah, that’s me. You can find me doing that all the time. No, I agree.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>As a childless adult, I’m judging.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>I’m just saying, right. I mean, I’m just saying that I think, in the phones discourse, we’re not always really distinguishing clearly between what are we saying are, like, individualized harms and, like, downstream negative consequences.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Because I’m in — I mean, on the one level, yes, clearly, I think almost everybody at the margin is, like, on their phone — myself included — is on their phone a little bit too much and should, like, talk to somebody or exercise or fucking go to sleep or something like that.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But there’s also this question of the macro impact on society, right? Of shifting to a world in which we are getting all this, like, app-based communication. People are dating differently. We talked about one thing, the media — like, you changing your media consumption habits won’t change the fact that The Media has been fundamentally altered by smartphones and social media, and we’re not gonna uninvent it, so...</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>I actually think that, you know — this is hot take prediction coming in. I think that, like, reduced smartphone use and, like, increased use of more dumb phone technology is gonna become, like, a classic signifier. Yeah. This is my take.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>So I’ll be — I’ll be a working class champion.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>You will be a working class champion scrolling on Twitter on your deathbed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Just tweeting, tweeting all the time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jerusalem Demsas: </span></strong><span>Well, if you enjoyed this conversation, please subscribe to </span><em><span>The Argument</span></em><span>. Tell your friends about it. Like, comment, and have a happy July 4th.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><strong><span>Matthew Yglesias: </span></strong><span>Happy birthday, America. underline;">poll</a><span> supposedly showing “socialism gaining ground with young voters.” But I don’t believe it. Young people may be more receptive to the </span><em>word</em><span> socialism, but that’s only because right-wingers constantly use that word to smear policies that have nothing to do with real socialism — i.e., government ownership of the means of production.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The fact is that very few Americans — even among politicians who call themselves “democratic socialists” — are really socialists. What many, I’d say a majority, of Americans support is what Europeans call social democracy — an ideology that is OK with living in a mostly market-driven economic system in which some people make much more money than others, but one that advocates policies to tame markets and inequality with progressive taxation, safety net programs, and regulations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">America already has an extensive range of social-democratic policies, although they are weaker than those in most other rich countries. And sustaining social democracy — indeed, making U.S. social democracy stronger — has very broad support, even among Republicans. Actual socialism, by contrast, has little public appeal.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Why, then, does it look as if socialism is on the rise? Mainly because right-wing propagandists continually smear social democratic policies as socialist, trying to make popular, mainstream policy ideas sound extreme. And some Americans who are basically social democrats in effect respond by saying, “Well, if that’s socialism, I guess I’m OK with socialism.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Right-wingers often try to portray social democratic policies as somehow un-American. But social democracy is as American as sliced bread, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a56767f4-01e7-4147-b8a0-5be3dcacc51d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">invented in 1928</a><span>. The Social Security Act, which created a safety net for the disabled and the unemployed as well as retirees, was passed just a few years later, in 1935. A national minimum wage was established in 1938. The big healthcare programs, Medicare and Medicaid, weren’t established until 1965 — but even that was 60 years ago.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So very few Americans even remember a nation that didn’t have a large, expensive social safety net — albeit one with some big holes in it. (In Texas, 19 percent of the population under 65 and 14 percent of children lack health insurance.)</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Progressive taxation has also been around for a very long time. When people say that they favor socialism, surely what they are often really saying is that they are angry about the rise of oligarchy. They are </span><em>not</em><span> demanding a dictatorship of the proletariat.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>And while there are, of course, left-wing radicals in America, they have no realistic prospect of getting their way. So it’s important to understand what the current uproar over socialism is really about. Allegiance at the start of the day. (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cf00166e-4474-48c6-9266-93bcbcf22f02?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Boston Globe</a><span>/Contributor via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I was at a couple of education events in the spring that all featured very smart, very achievement-oriented people talking about how to address the national crisis in basic reading and math attainment. A common lament was that politicians and pundits are simply not focused enough on the question of whether kids are learning the basics, preferring to fire off hot takes about culture war topics. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is a view that I very much sympathize with and have articulated over the years. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That said, I’ve also been in a bunch of conversations about things like Noah Smith’s essay on the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/da73a801-404e-469c-a7b8-3dab254d38a3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">need for a revival of American liberal nationalism</a><span> or Jerusalem Demsas’s take about how </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/247e7fdd-85b3-4793-92b1-fc866059f2ad?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">you have to love America in order to save it</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I broadly agree with these takes. But I also find that they’re a little bit lacking in specificity. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I know that Rob Sand, who’s running for governor in Iowa, does things like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/522cef80-8b03-4592-8779-144fe3bec2d9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">open town halls by having everyone sing “America the Beautiful.”</a><span> A friend described Sand as the Daniel Day-Lewis of politics: He understood quite some time ago that trends in Democratic Party politics were going one way and political trends in Iowa were going another, and he fully committed to a hyper-distinctive post-partisan Iowa-as-fuck persona. He never breaks character, and he not only performs the patriotic ritual, he makes it seem natural. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But if liberals want to embrace American patriotism, that has to mean more than just clicking “like” and “share” on columns that express a second-order thesis that it would be desirable to see more liberal patriotism. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">You need to actually do something specific, the way Sand does. I think Democrats should actually do some patriotism.</p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Pledging allegiance </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s a House bill called the “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/53578aa2-474d-4b5b-b2c5-7815b93ed0e4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Promoting American Patriotism In Our Schools Act</a><span>,” which is sponsored by Dale Strong of Alabama and co-sponsored by a handful of other Republicans. It would require public schools receiving federal Elementary and Secondary Education Act funds to “recite the Pledge of Allegiance to the Flag of the United States of America at the beginning of each school day.” It then also, to ensure conformity with free speech law, specifies that students must be allowed to opt out of pledging without penalty. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">My (private) K-8 school opened every day with the Pledge of Allegiance, and I later went to a more progressive high school that did not. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This obviously did not make a huge difference in practice, but it does set a different kind of tone. Of course, as a fussy writer and former philosophy student, I’ve always found the idea of pledging allegiance to a </span><em>flag</em><span> a little bit odd. A flag is a symbol of a thing, not a thing. Historically, the design of the flag has changed many times as a result of the accession of new states, and it’s not like people are switching allegiances when the flag changes. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But it is what it is. The text says that we are pledging allegiance not just to the flag but also “to the republic for which it stands,” which seems like the important part. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And I think if you’re going to be patriotic, then you ought to be loyal to the American republic. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We’re currently in a funny place where I think if I were to say “Democrats should promote the idea that people should be loyal to the American republic,” that would be considered an incredibly lukewarm take. But it’s not surprising or confusing to anyone that all the sponsors on the pledge bill are Republicans. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Yet, historically, this pledge to the flag and to the republic for which it stands is the conventional ritual. So isn’t Representative Strong just right about this? Again, I’m not saying students should be hauled into detention for refusing to engage in coerced speech. But most people tend to go along to get along. Defaults matter, and it seems to me that promoting a default of loyalty to the United States of America is a totally reasonable function for a public school system.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I also think that Democrats in particular increasingly need to ask themselves what they think a public school system is for. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Voucherizing the public school system is unpopular, and opposing that is often one of red state Democrats’ best issues. But Democrats struggle to articulate an actual purpose for these public institutions. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One such purpose, of course, should be student achievement. But that really has to be achievement at the low end. I don’t think it’s really credible to deny that affluent educated parents could just take the money and secure good education for our own kids. The people who’d be failed by a privatized solution are the kinds of kids who private schools would just try to screen out. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Lifting up students at the low end is an important cause. But I don’t think you can really talk about public education in a clear way without talking about the civic function of schools, and that should include cultivating a positive national identity. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Sweet land of liberty </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Marian Anderson was one of the most famous American singers of the 1930s. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>She was also African American, which greatly impacted her ability to tour and perform in the American South. This reached a head in 1939, when her manager tried to get her booked to perform at Constitution Hall run by the Daughters of the American Revolution here in Washington, D.C. They said no, upholding a color bar against Black performers. The D.C. Board of Education </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2dcc5efa-ea4f-4471-a684-343506e567f5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">also denied permission</a><span> to use the Central High School auditorium as a venue. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The N.A.A.C.P. decided to use this as an organizing opportunity and started a big campaign to pressure DAR to let Anderson sing. Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from the organization and led thousands of others to join her in doing so. Franklin Roosevelt was legendarily hyper-cautious about embracing civil rights issues, but he was persuaded that this one was a winner and his Interior Secretary Harold Ickes gave permission to organize an open-air concert on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For her first song, Anderson performed “My Country, ‘Tis of Thee,” the one about how America is a sweet land of liberty.  </p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/13e19c03-c05f-465f-813b-ba2960e601e8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/mAONYTMf2pk" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The concert was a huge deal, and it’s not a coincidence that 24 years later, Martin Luther King Jr., also speaking from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, closed his “I Have a Dream” speech with the same song: </p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #04B2A5;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This will be the day when all of God’s children will be able to sing with new meaning. “My country, ‘tis of thee, sweet land of liberty, of thee I sing. Land where my fathers died, land of the pilgrim’s pride, from every mountainside, let freedom ring.” And if America is to be a great nation, this must become true. So let freedom ring from the prodigious hilltops of New Hampshire. Let freedom ring from the mighty mountains of New York. Let freedom ring from the heightening Alleghenies of Pennsylvania. Let freedom ring from the snow-capped Rockies of Colorado. Let freedom ring from the curvaceous slopes of California. But not only that. Let freedom ring from Stone Mountain of Georgia. Let freedom ring from Lookout Mountain of Tennessee. Let freedom ring from every hill and molehill of Mississippi, from every mountainside. Let freedom ring!</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a conventional progressive point here that true patriots have always worked to improve their country rather than just be complacent about it. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But I also think it’s worth taking this whole sequence of events seriously. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Anderson is singing the song somewhat ironically. Her point was that to a considerable extent, America was in fact </span><em>not</em><span> a land of liberty. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Yet the performance worked, because people all across the country were taught to sing it non-ironically. Some people probably noticed the mismatch between the stated ideal and the reality; lots of people probably didn’t and just took it at face value. Yet it’s precisely because people grew up sincerely believing that America was a sweet land of liberty that gave the performance its punch. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If everyone had been raised to think of the United States as a country built on stolen land, enslaved labor, and genocide, then there’s actually no dissonance to resolve — a white person would simply think he had a pretty good deal in life.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s clearly a view that’s had a lot of influence over American educational practice that if you tell everyone how terrible everything is, that will inspire them to be activists for change. But most people just don’t care that much about politics and never will — you’re just fostering cynicism, fatalism, and selfishness in a way that’s totally at odds with the practice of Lincoln or King or anyone else who’s ever accomplished anything. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">America the beautiful </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But to return from the realm of instrumentality, it’s worth saying that America is a pretty awesome country. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The notion of the United States as a sweet land of liberty did not fully reflect the reality of 1939. But it wasn’t some kind of crazy cynical lie on a par with North Korea’s claim to be a democratic people’s republic. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The United States </span><em>really was</em><span> founded by a lot of religious dissenters and was genuinely a global pioneer in promoting pluralism and electoral democracy. It’s good and correct to say that the United States fell short of its ideals, but I think it’s also important to talk about the part where heroes fought to make the country live up to them and about the ways in which Americans have, through history, lived up to them. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And if you think about the recent history of the United States, there’s something blinkered about viewing the existence of racial tension and ethnic conflict as a distinctive fact of American life rather than a tragic but banal aspect of the human condition. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>People from all around the world are constantly trying to move here because the United States is a good place to live. The United States has the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/81c57de4-0c8c-402b-871f-db9346a5cee2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">highest median living standards</a><span> in the world outside of a handful of very small countries like Norway. We have probably the freest speech you’ll find anywhere. We have a robust and longstanding civic culture of integration, where the children and grandchildren of immigrants can also lay claim to being the metaphorical children of the founding fathers of the country. We landed humans on the Moon, we split the atom, we have </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b458b6ab-5e94-4b68-bc8a-684632b353ec?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">the most Nobel Prize winners</a><span>, we developed the best Covid vaccines, we created the internet, and we’re at the leading edge of artificial intelligence. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Americans are not the absolute number one most tolerant people with regard to who we are willing to welcome as neighbors, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8b1282cb-ac2c-470a-b53b-9f6e5f7ce058?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">but we’re way up there</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is basically what schools should teach kids. Not that America is or ever was perfect, but that relative to other actually existing places, the United States has pretty consistently been a beacon of opportunity and freedom without rival. Everyone should sing the songs and pledge the pledges.</p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Learning from our forebears</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When I took the history of early-modern moral philosophy in college, the professor told our class that we should try not to read the authors too skeptically. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">She didn’t mean that we should accept everything they said as true and correct — she was prepared to grant that we were all smart people who understood how to read a text critically. Her view was that studying the history of philosophy was a worthwhile undertaking. But the value of the undertaking is not to go through some essays written a long time ago by guys using somewhat unfamiliar language and talking about somewhat unfamiliar questions and just dunk on them. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The value is in trying to understand what these major thinkers of history brought to the table and why they’re interesting. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And I would really encourage us Democrats to build a public culture where we undertake our assessment of the great characters of American history in that spirit. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s easy to say that F.D.R.’s internment of Japanese Americans was bad and Ulysses Grant’s blind eye to corruption was bad and Andrew Jackson’s Trail of Tears was bad and Thomas Jefferson owning slaves was bad. Because all that stuff is really bad! </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s also genuinely important and interesting to understand how F.D.R. pulled the country out of the Great Depression and persuaded a largely unwilling nation to come to Europe’s aid. Jefferson wrote an incredible charter of human freedom. Jackson popularized our modern understanding of democracy. Grant saved the country. There’s nothing wrong with criticizing these figures, but it quickly becomes self-congratulatory and lame to gas yourself up compared to the heroic figures of the past just because you have conventional contemporary ethical views. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Part of constructing a paradigm of patriotic education should be making sure we have an inclusive canon of heroic figures to talk about so it’s not just a procession of white guys with a “too bad about the racism” asterisk. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it’s genuinely not hard to do this, and I think Donald Trump’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/da01cf86-46e5-4a5d-85a4-c41518c269d2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Garden of American Heroes</a><span> list is a broadly reasonable gesture in that direction. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Patriotism is good. America’s destiny is inextricably tied up with the fate of liberalism around the world, and Democrats shouldn’t just pay lip service to those ideas — we should promote them in concrete ways. </p><p More broadly, if you believe that nation-states are legitimate entities, then you must admit that countries have an inherent right to preserve their cultures in amber by shutting themselves off to immigration, if they want to. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But MAGA has already lost that battle. America is not North Korea; we’re not even Japan or Sweden. 79% of Americans say that immigration is good for the country overall; they say this even knowing that immigration will cause some long-term cultural changes. The cultural preservation argument against immigration is a lost cause, no matter how desperately its proponents shriek and bluster and threaten. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">At the same time, Democrats must be extremely wary of embracing open borders simply out of pure reaction to MAGA nativism. Americans don’t want to let just anyone in; they want people to come legally, and they want to admit people who earn enough money to contribute positively to the economy. If Democrats simply respond to each electoral victory by throwing open the borders and turning a blind eye to illegal immigration, the American people will continue to respond by intermittently electing xenophobes. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the age of low fertility, America desperately needs to be </span><em>smart </em><span>about its immigration strategy. auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In what would be major news except for all the other disasters happening, Donald Trump has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fed4ba54-4fb2-4c38-bbff-7f06d44c1ae3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">declined to renew the USMCA</a><span> — the successor to the North American Free Trade Agreement — which he himself negotiated. This puts businesses on notice that tariff-free shipments within North America, which NAFTA supposedly made permanent, may go away.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Some commentators have dismissed this as no big deal, because Trump’s successor will probably reverse his decision and make the USMCA permanent after all. However, this misses the point of such agreements. Before NAFTA went into effect, North American tariffs were already low. The average tariff imposed by the US on imports from Mexico was only 2 percent. But NAFTA gave more than tariff relief. It gave, or seemed to give, certainty: businesses could invest in border-spanning supply chains confident that they would be able to use these chains for many years to come.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Or, as it turns out, not, if we have a U.S. president who doesn’t care about breaking promises.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Bloomberg ran a segment about all of this, with a substantial part coming from an interview I had with David Westin a few weeks ago:</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/c0bb27a0-7dce-4512-b9bb-9e96dee870fd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/nIhm4sqmOkc" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Transcript</strong><span>:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin </span></strong><span>We start with the poster child for North American trade, the auto industry. Since the USMCA’s predecessor, NAFTA, came into effect over 30 years ago, autos have been at the center of negotiations. The reason is simple. The industry is tightly integrated across northern and southern US borders, borders like the one between Detroit, Michigan and Windsor, Ontario. This is the brand new Gordie Howe International Bridge that spans the Detroit River, separating the Motor City from Windsor. It was named for the famed hockey player who was born in Canada but crossed the border to lead the Detroit Red Wings to four Stanley Cups. Canada paid for the bridge, but now President Trump has put its opening on hold, which in itself is unlikely to divide the two cities’ economies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Krugman </span></strong><span>Those are not really separate cities. There just happens to be a borderline through them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin </span></strong><span>Economist Paul Krugman won the Nobel Prize for his work on trade.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Krugman </span></strong><span>Stuff does go back and forth. There’s a tremendous amount of specialization, which is good for everybody. It reduces costs, increases efficiency.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin: </span></strong><span>One of the companies benefiting from that back and forth trade is Linamar, a manufacturer with headquarters outside of Toronto. Jim Jarrell is its CEO.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jarrell </span></strong><span>So we’re 60 years old and really I think when you look at Linamar, we’re an advanced manufacturing and product design technology company with 37,000 people global, 87 facilities around the world.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin:</span></strong><span> When we talk about the auto part of Linamar’s business, how much of your production goes across either the Canadian-U.S. border or the U.S.-Mexican border or for that matter Canada-Mexico?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jarrell </span></strong><span>I would say a ton. There is so much interconnection, integration between it. And I think we’ve demonstrated this before. We have one part that we do for an OEM customer, two OEMs in the U.S. and the original part that we get is a forging that comes into Mexico, which goes into the U.S. to get some further processing, comes into Canada for further processing, back to the U.S. for further processing, over to Canada where we do the sort of final assembly, and then that gets distributed back into the U.S.as well as Mexico and Canadian auto plants. So again, you can see this full integration Of this, you know, supply chain in the automotive North American area. And one thing we say is you can’t unbake the omelet, right?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Manufacturing has become a regional game.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin:</span></strong><span> Shannon O’Neil is the director of studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, author of the book, “The Globalization Myth, Why Regions Matter,” and a Bloomberg opinion contributor.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>O’Neil </span></strong><span>The strength, frankly, of the U.S. auto industry is really a North American auto industry. It is that because cars and car parts are produced across Mexico, Canada, and the United States, they are strong, they are competitive and they’re affordably priced. And it’s that connection, those supply chains across North America that are important for autos. important for all kinds of manufacturing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin:</span></strong><span> Given how the, I’ll call it, North American auto industry has evolved, is it even possible to cut off imports and exports of automobiles and auto parts between the United States and Canada and/or Mexico?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>O’Neil </span></strong><span>There’s a real question if we didn’t have NAFTA, if we didn’t have USMCA, would we have a North American car industry at all, if we didn’t have the economies of scale of production that have now developed over North America? Could we bring back just a U.S.-produced car? Sure, we could, but it would be a much more expensive car. It would likely be a less innovative car in terms of the parts that go into it. And it would be really hard to compete against imports from Japan, South Korea, Europe,and other places.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin: </span></strong><span>The USMCA may have been a win-win for auto industry companies like Linamar and for American consumers, but it hasn’t necessarily addressed President Trump’s underlying concerns about the balance of trade between the U.S. and either Canada or Mexico. For 2025, the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico was nearly $200 billion, with Canada about $46 billion. But O’Neill says regardless of the trade deficit, President Trump is underestimating the extent to which the U.S. needs trade both ways with both Canada and Mexico.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Jarrell </span></strong><span>What we see is a big influx of goods coming from Mexico to the United States. It’s now the number one exporter to the United States, or U.S. importer. In part, that’s replacing Chinese trade. In part, that is just the strength of North American supply chains and the back and forth of goods and services that move there. But we also need to remember that Mexico and Canada are the number one export markets for U.S. companies, for U.S. products that go out into the world. So we are very dependent on them as they are on us.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin</span></strong><span>: Another concern often expressed by President Trump when it comes to trade, particularly in the auto industry, is the loss of jobs, something Krugman admits is real, but not really the fault of the USMCA. What do you say to people from my home state of Michigan who hear President Trump say, you know, that’s a good idea? We’re going to actually have some barriers put up so that we have more of those plants in Michigan, in Ohio, so we have better jobs? Because we have lost a lot of those jobs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Krugman </span></strong><span>We have lost a lot of jobs, but it’s not mostly because of NAFTA, right? I still call it NAFTA, sorry, it’s a lot easier given that Trump keeps changing the name. But anyway, do we have fewer manufacturing jobs in the United States, do we have fewer auto jobs in the United States because of the USMCA? I think that’s highly doubtful. The idea that somehow turning our back on the world here is going to add jobs is probably wrong.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin</span></strong><span>: And then there’s China, not part of USMCA negotiations, but always a specter in the room.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Krugman </span></strong><span>China is looming over all of these negotiations and this real worry about China selling products into the United States using Mexico or Canada as a backdoor in, right, getting the benefits of free trade without actually being party to the negotiations and to the agreements. And so what we’ve seen is Mexico in particular push back against Chinese imports, which have grown dramatically over the last five years into Mexico. Some of this are cars and car parts and the like, some are other electronics and the like. So we’ve seen them push back to really support North America. And as we get into the USMCA negotiations, China and this idea of transshipment, of shipping parts in through Mexico to the United States, is a big part of the conversation. And one can see, and I think all parties are open to, creating a real North America fortress vis-a-vis China, vis-a-vis other imports from around the world.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’re in a world now where, as we’ve seen, interdependence can be weaponized. We used to think that that was something we did to other countries, but now we find out that other countries do it to us, too. So the idea that you need to maintain capacity in your own country or in reliable allies for strategically important stuff is now very, very real. I am really reluctant to be where I am right now, but I do think that conditional tariffs on Chinese cars are probably going to be necessary. I don’t think that the Europeans can allow their auto industry to be totally hollowed out. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, there’s some compromise here. Probably totally trying to shut Chinese cars out of the market is going to be a bad thing, be very costly to consumers. But on the other hand, I’ve been shocked not only by my own change of mind, but by some of my colleagues, people who are longtime advocates of globalization and free trade who are saying, okay, Europe needs to do some, really, if you like, it’s national security, it’s market disruption, to just allow something as big as the European auto industry to just be overrun, even if consumers would benefit for a while, it’s not 20 years ago anymore. We really do need to rethink, which is a long way from saying that we should have tariffs on everything or that the Europeans should have tariffs on everything. But a much more interventionist position has become really hard to avoid.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin</span></strong><span>: But for all the concern about trade deficits and jobs and putting sand in the gears of the North American auto industry, those most closely involved have one concern above all. I would say certainty has got to be the prize award that we’ve got to be chasing here. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Krugman </span></strong><span>I just think that is absolutely critical to have that. The great virtue of this whole world’s trade system that the United States basically set up after World War II was that it provided, it wasn’t just that their tariffs were low, though that’s important, but even more important, things were predictable. I would almost prefer that Trump put on more tariffs on Canada and Mexico, but committed to keep them in place, than have rolling negotiations where every year you don’t know what next year will be like.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Westin</span></strong><span>: If you were advising President Trump how to win the negotiation with Canada and Mexico, what would you advise him?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Krugman </span></strong><span>The USMCA is an easy case because this is not, there is no trade conflict here except in Trump’s mind. All of the things we’re talking about are not a problem for the USMCA. We shouldn’t be worried about being dependent on Canadian aluminum. They’ve got the hydropower, they’ve got the cheap electricity, they’re right next to us. They speak almost the same language. This is not an issue. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We are not really worried about the U.S. auto industry being hollowed out by Mexican auto production because Mexican auto production is part of an integrated system, which actually probably makes the U.S. more competitive. No, the USMCA, or maybe just rename it NAFTA and go back to the original purpose, which is this is a case where it really makes sense to have a true free trade area. In fact, if I could, I would say this is a case where we should go beyond free trade to a European Union style customs union with free movement of goods across borders, no checks at all, a common external frontier for goods. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>We have a real problem with China. The problem with Mexico and Canada is just a figment of the president’s imagination.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. stand together during a “Fighting Oligarchy” tour stop at the Collins Center for the Arts on the University of Maine campus on May 24, 2026. (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/706d4a66-46dc-495e-8e36-be89dabbcf7d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Joe Raedle</a><span>/Staff via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Almost all of the questions today were about Democrats’ ongoing tea party moment in primaries, which got me thinking about the actual Tea Party of the Obama years. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the time, the Tea Party talked an enormous amount about government spending and budget deficits,</span><strong> </strong><span>and mainstream Republicans largely treated it as a movement about fiscal conservatism. A desire to harness Tea Party energy was part of why Mitt Romney picked Paul Ryan as his running mate and challenged Obama on a platform of steep spending cuts rather than Moderate Massachusetts Mitt pragmatism. Around this time, I worked with Vanessa Williamson’s husband and I knew Theda Skocpol from college, so I was aware of the book the two of them wrote in 2013 called “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/df2f4da4-5a8a-4d97-800b-1c8205acabc2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>The Tea Party and the Remaking of Republican Conservatism</span></a><span>.” It was a sociological deep dive into Tea Party activism and featured the striking and contrarian claim that </span><em><span>actually</span></em><span> the number one issue motivating the movement was immigration. Very few people in 2013 agreed with that, but after watching Donald Trump’s 2016 primary win, I think everyone familiar with this literature reached the conclusion that Williamson and Skocpol were right all along. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I raise this because, while we’ve had a ton of takes about what is driving the restive left on the Democratic side, I </span><em><span>don’t</span></em><span> think we’ve had anything equivalent to </span><span>Williamson and Skocpol in the sense of a genuinely good-faith, curiosity-motivated look at what’s going on. This is not to say I have my own secret theory. I also don’t want to overread the analogy. Just because the Tea Party seemed to be about one thing and turned out to be about another doesn’t mean the left insurgency is like that. It may just be that it’s actually a bad analogy. But I do want to draw the distinction between disinterested scholarly inquiry and factional or partisan combat. A lot of influential figures in right-wing politics really wanted it to be the case that the Tea Party was about widespread demand for entitlement cuts, and they successfully imposed that interpretation on the world for a period of years until it all blew up in their face. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-5f7?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=284361510" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>lindamc:</span></a><span> I’m a Common Sense Dem at the end of my tether. I split my time between DC, with an incoming socialist mayor, and Ann Arbor MI, where socialists are seeking to unseat the local government that has (as noted in a recent mailbag) finally started building here. Everyone knows about the Senate race 😩. Many/most youngs I know are self-described socialists with little/no understanding of what that means in historic terms, and the overwhelming majority of my fellow olds are Heather Cox Richardsonians. Virtually every social gathering I attend features someone making a glib, ignorant complaint about data centers. A “swing dancing in the park” event I attended a few days ago started out with pronouns and cultural appropriation and never made it to demonstrating actual dance steps. Things seem to somehow get worse and worse.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>How do you cope with this? Despite fighting hard against it, I feel something like actual despair a lot of the time.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m feeling a little bit untethered myself this summer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But one thing that I try to remind myself of is that a lot of what I am experiencing ambiently is not so much a real political trend as the output of the extraordinary New York-centricity of the national media. </span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Imagine if the whole national press were concentrated in San Francisco. You’d have stories talking about how Dan Lurie is the most popular mayor in America. But they’d also be talking about how his successes were really prefigured by Brooke Jenkins. And about how part of why both Lurie and Jenkins are succeeding is that they belong to a broader reform faction in San Francisco politics that’s winning Board of Supervisors races and contesting internal Democratic Party offices and poised to make a run at the school board. You’d see Matt Mahan down the road in San Jose. You’d talk about how his gubernatorial bid fizzled, but you’d also know Tom Steyer’s leftist gubernatorial bid fizzled, too. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And if the press were a little less New York-centric, we’d hear more about Chicago, too: The left won power there, and it’s been an embarrassing failure they don’t talk about anymore.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An electoral backlash to Mayor Brandon Johnson is clearly coming, and the only real question is whether it will be a retreat to status quo mainstream Democratic governance or if we’ll see a more dramatic form of pushback. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fbfe894b-e9bc-40f8-b7bd-808d7d9221d9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>A City That Works</span></a><span>, which began as a Chicago-focused Substack very much aligned with Slow Boring values, has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/914ca6df-bcfd-496b-bb40-daeed9cf2724?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>now launched a PAC</span></a><span> that is going to try to get not just a good mayor but some good City Council members elected to bring some of the San Francisco magic to the Windy City. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>From a D.C. perspective, I am sad that Kenyan McDuffie lost. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it’s possible that the only way to move forward from where D.C. was under Muriel Bowser’s third term was to take this detour. Voters in the city wanted change, and McDuffie read as continuity. Something I tried to say to people (mostly unsuccessfully) is that the direction of change matters. But now that there’s been a regime change in the city, the opening exists to articulate a smart reformist critique of the status quo and to find some outsider figures to run for office on a smart program. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even in New York, where a lot of attention has been paid to Darializa Avila Chevalier’s continued advocacy for prison abolition, it’s clear that Zohran Mamdani understands perfectly well that a successful mayor needs a safe city. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As someone who was engaged in a lot of very nasty disputes about policing in the summer of 2020, I am personally </span><em><span>extremely</span></em><span> annoyed that the left’s surrender on this has taken the form of acting peevish about anyone raising their old tweets. I would love for someone to write on the internet, “You know what, I disagree with Matt Yglesias about a lot of things, but not only was he correct about police defunding, he was gutsy to say so at a time when it was controversial.” To the best of my knowledge, nobody at all has ever done that even as virtually the whole left has moved toward my view. So I’m aggravated about the situation and I find the discourse — especially in N.Y.C.-centric media — to be fairly despair-inducing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But while the situation is somewhat grave, that’s mostly just because politics is important and the stakes always feel high. The actual trends across the country are fairly mixed and there are reasons for both optimism and pessimism. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Where I do give the left credit is on two related points where I think there are valuable lessons to be learned. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One is that they have real team spirit. Bernie Sanders has been tireless and fairly selfless in touring the country to elevate the profile of Bernie-aligned candidates and help them raise money. Then his more successful acolytes like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez pay it forward and do the same. And even the different members of this movement </span><em><span>say they are members of a movement</span></em><span> rather than insisting that each one is a beautiful unique snowflake. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The other point is that they are not terrified of losing. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s easy to imagine a world where Graham Platner’s campaign ended up looking like an embarrassing failure rather than a striking success. And Steyer’s campaign really was an embarrassing failure. But having failed in an embarrassing way with Steyer, they just moved on to some wins in New York and then talked a lot about those wins. I know people who were involved in directing money to Baldacci and then immediately felt like they were in hot water for being involved in something that failed. But the fact is that he came very close to winning his primary and he was the right candidate. It’s too bad that more wasn’t done to support him (and that he’s not more mediagenic), but you need to try things. And you need to have some grace for people who try things and it doesn’t work out. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-5f7?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=284461831" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">lwdlyndale:</a><span> The Times finally decided to write something </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/94b7fb25-cf2d-4d22-b366-719ad6b4208b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">about Andy Beshear and his bid for the White House</a><span>: Do you think there’s any chance we could see some real #Andymentum in the 2028 cycle, or do you think, like most of the chattering classes, that he’s obviously doomed?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">On the subject of trying things, I think the problem with Beshear-type politicians is that they are excessively risk-averse. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a level where, yes, Beshear seems like a strong candidate on paper, especially for primary voters who say electability is their top priority. But to beat Republicans, he needs the nomination first. So the easy strategy is to just emphasize his winning credentials in a non-specific way and say he’s not a far-left socialist but also not say anything that could alienate any mainstream Democrats whose support he needs. The problem with this is that it’s boring and indistinct and vague and ultimately leaves him with no firm footing when inevitable misfortunes come his way. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">An alternative strategy would be to:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Pick some positions that are popular with the median voter in Kentucky but unpopular with most Democratic Party elected officials. </p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Articulate those positions clearly and say they make you a different kind of Democrat and that’s why you can win nationally. </p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Make the case that the path to progressive goals is to be a 50-state party that can expand Medicaid, crush MAGA, and enact big durable change in the country. </p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This will probably not work! The odds are good that step one just kills you. But it </span><em>might</em><span> work. If he tried it, I would say nice things about him. And so would other people. And some others would say mean things about him. And there would be a proper argument about it. The problem is that if you’re Beshear, the default strategy might be to run a lame campaign that stirs no controversy and fails for obvious reasons but sets you up for a cabinet job. What I want to see is him try a higher variance strategy where he really explains what people in Kentucky think and care about and where he challenges presidential primary voters to care about winning in places like that.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-5f7?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=284397673" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Jesse Ewiak:</a><span> It’s the day after Election Day in 2026.</span></strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Graham Platner has won by 6 to 7 points.</strong></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Abdul El-Sayed has won by 3 to 4 points.</strong></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>How cooked is the moderate wing in the upcoming 2028 primaries and should they just put their power behind somebody like Ossoff instead of attempting to slam Shapiro or someone similar through the primaries?</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I think this is the wrong way to think about it. What is “the moderate wing” at this point, really? To me the worst way to think about 2028 is to start with the idea that there’s A.O.C. and everyone else is “moderate,” so Democrats need to try our hardest to elect a moderate (i.e. not A.O.C.) and therefore decide if we should get behind Shapiro or Newsom or Ossoff or who. What I want to do is start with the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fe4e582c-89ce-43ea-a738-8f74999b6c00?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">values of the Common Sense Democrat Manifesto</a><span> and then back whichever candidate best embodies those values. I am open to that person being Shapiro or Ossoff or someone else or even A.O.C. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I want to be a policy demander and see some elements of the field try to move toward my views. </p><p class="button-wrapper"
